title: Tracking progress on the path to IBM Quantum Starling
content: Quantum Research Blog Tracking progress on the path to IBM Quantum Starling Advances across parallel technology areas are laying the groundwork for fault-tolerant quantum computing by the end of the decade. Date 11 Nov 2026 Authors Matthias Steffen Matthew Marwick Topics Error Correction & Mitigation Systems Share this blog Was this blog post helpful? Yes No IBM will deliver IBM Quantum Starling, capable of running 100 million hard operations on 200 qubits, in 2029. IBM has validated c-coupler technology for enabling dense, non-local qubit connectivity. Improvements to IBM’s qLDPC code have made it possible to have only five connections between qubits instead of six. IBM’s Relay-BP decoder now meets Starling performance requirements while lowering compute overhead for decoding. With l-couplers, modular cryogenics, and cryogenic ASIC control electronics, IBM has demonstrated the modular scaling essential for fault-tolerant systems. IBM is building the world’s first fault-tolerant quantum computer, IBM Quantum Starling. Slated to launch in 2029, Starling will be capable of running quantum circuits comprising 100 million quantum operations on 200 qubits. The framework for Starling was described in a 2025 paper , which presented a path to achieve fault tolerance by creating hardware to implement the bivariate bicycle quantum low-density parity check (qLDPC) error correction codes introduced by IBM in a 2024 Nature publication . Critically, the code is implemented in a modular fashion to enable scalability beyond what could be achieved with a monolithic architecture. The modular architecture detailed in the paper offers an order of magnitude reduction in resource requirements compared to prior approaches. For the same logical error rate, Starling’s qLDPC architecture requires about 10x fewer physical qubits. It is constructed by assembling modules that each contain a quantum memory and logical processing unit (LPU), which allows logic operations on the memory. The modules have universal adapters that allow them to be connected using l-couplers. Additionally, sophisticated modular cryogenic and control systems house and run the modules at ultra-cold operating temperatures. This diagram shows the components that will need to come together for IBM Quantum Starling. Below, we provide an update on significant technical advances toward Starling, broken down into six categories. These steps forward are being delivered in parallel, though not in isolation — lessons from one component influence the progress being made on the others. Taken together, the work outlined below represents major progress toward building Starling and delivering on the promise of fault-tolerant quantum computing. Device physics IBM Quantum Loon was announced a year ago to demonstrate many of the key components needed to implement IBM’s qLDPC codes, including qubit reset circuits and “c-couplers” to link qubits across the chip, a prerequisite for establishing the six-way qubit connectivity needed to implement the qLDPC code. Since then, Loon was measured to have qubit relaxation times (T1) of about 200us with reset time constants of 20ns–40ns. Its gates had median error rates near 0.3%. The ultimate aim for Starling is to have T1 in the millisecond range and gate errors in the low 0.01% range. The physics of the device are designed to enable this low error rate. In fact, we routinely measure gate errors in the high 0.01% range on Heron and Nighthawk — going as low as 0.04%. Transferring coherence times from our test devices, which are currently in the single digit millisecond range, will also help facilitate lower error rates. It is also important to understand how much loss the c-coupler layers introduce so we can estimate gate error limits. The results here are also very promising. The resonators had quality factors above 10 million, which is beyond the goal needed for Starling. Adding to this, it was found that traversing c-coupler layers only resulted in a minimal reduction in quality factor, meaning it was possible to increase the number of c-coupler layers being used in the chip. Originally two were being used, but that has now increased to three with plans to reach four or more. Adding additional layers will enable more complex routing and can effectively shorten some of the longest connections c-couplers need to make. The results above verify that c-couplers are a viable approach to enabling non-local, dense connections for quantum processors. QPUs Advances have also been made in how quantum processing units (QPUs) can be put together. In particular, there have been two exciting developments related to overall device yield and complexity. First, improvements to the qLDPC code made it possible to have only five connections between qubits instead of six — while also delivering 20x-100x lower logical errors.
